title: Bartleby, the Scrivener
text:
The narrator is a comfortable, elderly lawyer with chambers on Wall Street, where he employs copyists to make handwritten copies of legal documents. Business is growing, so he hires a new one: Bartleby, pale, neat and silent. At first Bartleby copies enormous amounts, day and night, though mechanically and without cheer.

Then one day, asked to help check a copy against the original, Bartleby answers mildly: "I would prefer not to." The lawyer is stunned. Soon Bartleby prefers not to check anything, then not to run errands, and finally not to copy at all. He simply stands looking out the window at a blank brick wall. The lawyer discovers he has been living in the office.

The lawyer tries everything. He reasons, offers money, and orders him to leave. Bartleby prefers not to. Unable to bring himself to throw out a helpless man, the lawyer finally moves his own offices instead. The new tenants have Bartleby removed. When the lawyer visits, he offers to take Bartleby into his own home, and Bartleby prefers not to. He is taken to the Tombs prison as a vagrant.

There he refuses to eat and dies. Afterward the lawyer hears a rumor that Bartleby once worked in the Dead Letter Office in Washington, sorting letters meant for people who had died. "Ah Bartleby! Ah humanity!"
lesson: Some problems at work are really human crises that rules and incentives cannot reach. You may not be able to fix them, but you can still see the person and refuse to treat them as just a problem.
people: The lawyer narrator, Bartleby, Turkey, Nippers, Ginger Nut
source: Herman Melville, Bartleby, the Scrivener: A Story of Wall Street, 1853
